newsitem.title: USA: Saudi suspect at risk if plea deal revealed -lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Saudi suspect at risk if plea deal revealed -lawyer.

text.p: A Saudi suspect in the bombing that killed 19 U.S. airmen last June would be at risk if details of a plea agreement on an unrelated charge were made public, his lawyer told a court on Thursday.

At a U.S. District Court hearing, a judge postponed proceedings in the case and agreed to appoint a doctor to examine the defendant, Hani al-Sayegh, who is said by his lawyer to have suffered an asthma attack on Wednesday night.

The judge, Emmet Sullivan, ordered the hearing to resume on Wednesday. At that time, court papers indicate Sayegh will plead guilty to conspiracy to commit murder in an earlier, abortive, Anti-American plot in Saudi Arabia.

In exchange for a reduced sentence on those charges, Sayegh has said he would tell U.S. officials what he knows about the June 25 attack on Khobar Towers in Dhahran that killed 19 Air Force personnel and injured 500.

U.S. officials hope that Sayegh, 28, will help clarify whether the government of Iran was involved, as some Saudi officials have at some times said, or whether it was solely the work of Saudi dissidents opposed to the ruling royal family.
Sayegh's attorney joined the U.S. government in opposing the unsealing of the plea documents.
Several news organisations have urged the court to make public the agreement and accompanying proceedings, citing First Amendment freedoms and the public's right to know.

Disclosure of any details "would put my client at risk," the lawyer, Michael Wildes, told the judge. He did not elaborate in court on the risk to Sayegh, a Shi'ite Moslem described in Canadian court documents as a member of Saudi Hizbollah, or Party of God, a militant group backed by Iran.
Sullivan said it would be premature for him to consider the press request for unsealing, issued by the Washington Post, joined by CNN, ABC, NBC and CBS.
In ordering the medical examination, the judge, citing security concerns, said he would keep secret the name of the facility and the name of the court-appointed doctor.
He named Francis Carter, a well-known Washington public defender, as co-defence counsel, citing his experience in "high profile, sensational cases."
Sayegh, unshackled and wearing a white shirt and an earnest look, sat behind a 10-foot bulletproof plexiglass partition separating him from reporters and the public.

He listened intently as a court-appointed Arabic speaker translated the proceedings. When asked by the judge whether he was satisfied with his lawyers, Sayegh smiled broadly and nodded in assent. At the outset, he said he understood English "a little bit."

Sayegh was deported on Tuesday from Canada, where he was arrested in March on charges of posing a security risk. On Wednesday, he was charged in Washington with conspiring to kill Americans and involvement in "international terrorism."
Outside the courthouse, Wildes, the defence lawyer, said "measures have been taken" to protect Sayegh's wife and two young children who are still in Saudi Arabia.

Sayegh has been identified in Canadian court documents as the driver of a car that flashed a go-ahead signal for the bomb-laden truck involved in the attack on Khobar Towers. He has denied direct involvement in the bombing.
